summary: LLM API costs scale rapidly in production, but inference-time optimization techniques can reduce spend by 50–95% without changing model outputs or quality. The most impactful levers are prompt caching (up to 90% off repeated prefixes), semantic caching (eliminating redundant requests entirely), and model routing (sending simple tasks to cheaper models). A combined strategy using caching, compression, and right-sizing can realistically cut monthly API bills by 70–80% within a few weeks of engineering effort.

techniques.name: Prompt Caching (Provider-Native)
techniques.description: Stores the computed key-value tensors for repeated prompt prefixes server-side at the provider level. When the same prefix is sent again, the provider skips recomputing it and charges a deeply discounted cache-read rate instead of full input token price. Every major provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) now ships this natively with no code changes required beyond prompt ordering.
techniques.savings: 50–90% reduction on input tokens for cached prefixes; Anthropic charges ~10% of normal input price on cache hits
techniques.example: Place your 20,000-token RAG knowledge base or static system prompt at the very top of every request so the prefix stays identical across calls. Anthropic will cache it after the first request (min 1,024 tokens for Haiku, 2,048 for Sonnet/Opus) and charge ~90% less on all subsequent cache hits.

techniques.name: Semantic Caching
techniques.description: Caches full LLM responses keyed by the semantic meaning of the user query, not just exact text. When a new query is semantically similar to a cached one (e.g., 'What is your return policy?' vs 'How do I return an item?'), the cached response is returned instantly without hitting the LLM API at all, eliminating 100% of token costs for that request.
techniques.savings: 100% cost elimination for cache-hit requests; typical production hit rates of 30–45% in high-repetition query scenarios
techniques.example: Deploy GPTCache or Redis semantic cache in front of your API calls with a cosine similarity threshold of 0.92. In a customer support chatbot with repetitive queries, this can yield a 45% cache hit rate and reduce effective API costs by nearly half.

techniques.name: Model Routing
techniques.description: Classifies incoming requests by complexity and routes them to the cheapest model capable of handling them adequately. Simple tasks like classification, extraction, or FAQ lookup go to budget models (GPT-3.5, Claude Haiku, Gemini Flash), while complex reasoning or nuanced generation is reserved for frontier models. This is the highest-leverage technique when you have mixed workloads.
techniques.savings: 40–70% overall cost reduction depending on workload distribution; budget models cost 10–50x less than frontier models
techniques.example: Use a lightweight classifier to score query complexity 1–5, then route scores 1–2 to Claude Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 per M tokens), scores 3–4 to Claude Sonnet 4.6 ($3/$15), and only score 5 to Claude Opus 4.8 ($5/$25). A real-world implementation reported routing 70% of traffic to cheap models, cutting the blended per-token cost by over 60%.

techniques.name: Prompt Compression
techniques.description: Reduces the number of input tokens sent per request by removing redundant instructions, cutting few-shot examples, trimming verbose format instructions, and keeping system prompts concise. Structural changes like using bullet points instead of prose and removing filler phrases directly reduce input costs proportionally.
techniques.savings: 20–40% reduction in input token costs with no quality loss if done carefully
techniques.example: Audit your system prompt and cut it from 800 tokens to under 200 by replacing verbose format instructions with a single structured output schema. Replace 5 few-shot examples with 1 precise example. A 30% reduction in average prompt length translates directly to a 30% reduction in input token spend.

techniques.name: Output Constraints
techniques.description: Limits the number of tokens the model generates per response by setting max_tokens explicitly, using structured output formats (JSON schemas), and instructing the model to be concise. Since output tokens cost 4–5x more than input tokens on flagship models, reducing output length has an outsized cost impact.
techniques.savings: 30–50% reduction in output token costs; output tokens cost $10–15 per million vs $2–3 for input on flagship models
techniques.example: Set max_tokens=150 explicitly in every API call for classification or extraction tasks, and add 'Respond in JSON only, no explanation' to your prompt. This alone can cut output tokens by 50% on tasks where the model would otherwise pad its response with reasoning text.

techniques.name: Batch API Processing
techniques.description: Submits multiple requests as an asynchronous batch rather than individual real-time calls. Providers like Anthropic and OpenAI offer 50% discounts on batch API requests because they can process them during off-peak hours. Ideal for non-time-sensitive workloads like document processing, embeddings generation, evaluations, and data enrichment.
techniques.savings: 50% flat discount on all token costs for batched requests
techniques.example: Instead of processing 10,000 product descriptions in real-time, submit them via Anthropic's Message Batches API as a single batch job. At Sonnet 4.6 pricing, this drops the effective cost from $3/$15 per million tokens to $1.50/$7.50, saving 50% with zero engineering complexity beyond changing the API endpoint.

techniques.name: RAG Optimization and Reranking
techniques.description: Reduces the number of context tokens passed to the LLM in retrieval-augmented generation pipelines by retrieving more chunks initially, reranking them with a cheap cross-encoder model, and passing only the top-k most relevant chunks. This avoids stuffing the context window with loosely relevant documents that inflate token counts.
techniques.savings: 20–50% reduction in context tokens per RAG request depending on retrieval quality
techniques.example: Retrieve 20 chunks from your vector store, run them through a lightweight reranker (e.g., Cohere Rerank or a local cross-encoder), then pass only the top 5 chunks to the LLM. This can cut context tokens from 15,000 to 3,500 per query while improving answer quality due to higher-relevance context.

techniques.name: Quantized and Smaller Open-Source Models
techniques.description: Self-hosting quantized open-source models (e.g., 4-bit or 8-bit quantized Llama, Qwen, Gemma, or DeepSeek variants) eliminates per-token API costs entirely, replacing them with fixed GPU infrastructure costs. For high-volume workloads, the break-even point against API pricing is often reached at relatively modest request volumes.
techniques.savings: Up to 100% elimination of per-token API costs at scale; quantization reduces VRAM requirements by 50–75% vs full-precision models
techniques.example: Deploy Gemma 4 26B A4B (quantized) on a single 32GB unified-memory machine using vLLM as the inference server behind an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint. At high query volume, fixed GPU costs can be 80–90% cheaper than equivalent frontier model API spend.

techniques.name: Context Window Management and Conversation Pruning
techniques.description: Actively manages the conversation history sent with each request to avoid unnecessary token bloat. Strategies include summarizing older turns, sliding window approaches that drop the oldest messages, and storing long-term context in vector stores rather than in-context. Critical for multi-turn chat applications where context grows unboundedly.
techniques.savings: 30–60% reduction in input tokens for long multi-turn conversations
techniques.example: After every 10 conversation turns, use a cheap model (e.g., GPT-3.5 or Haiku) to summarize the conversation so far into 200 tokens, then replace the full history with that summary plus the last 2 turns. This keeps context under 1,000 tokens regardless of conversation length.

tools.name: LiteLLM
tools.description: Open-source proxy and SDK that provides a unified OpenAI-compatible API across 100+ LLM providers. Enables model routing, load balancing, fallbacks, spend tracking, and cost controls from a single interface. Can be self-hosted as a proxy server or used as a Python library.
tools.pricing_paid: Free open-source; LiteLLM Enterprise starts at custom pricing for SSO, advanced analytics

tools.name: GPTCache
tools.description: Open-source semantic caching library specifically designed for LLM applications. Supports exact-match and embedding-based similarity caching with pluggable vector stores (FAISS, Redis, Milvus). Integrates directly with LangChain and OpenAI SDK to transparently cache and return responses.

tools.name: Redis Semantic Cache
tools.description: Redis-native semantic caching solution using Redis Stack with vector similarity search. Stores LLM responses indexed by embedding vectors and returns cached answers for semantically similar queries. Works as middleware for any LLM provider and offers sub-millisecond cache lookup latency at scale.
tools.pricing_paid: Redis Cloud from $5/month; Redis Enterprise custom pricing

tools.name: Helicone
tools.description: LLM observability and proxy platform that logs all API calls, tracks token usage and costs per user/session/model, and provides caching (both exact and semantic), rate limiting, and prompt management. Sits as a one-line proxy change in front of OpenAI, Anthropic, or any provider.
tools.pricing_paid: Free up to 10,000 requests/month; Pro at $20/month; Team/Enterprise custom

tools.name: LangChain
tools.description: The most widely used LLM application framework, offering built-in caching (InMemoryCache, SQLiteCache, Redis), model abstraction layers, prompt template management, RAG pipeline components, and output parsers that help constrain token usage. Not a cost tool per se, but its abstractions make it easy to implement most optimization techniques.
tools.pricing_paid: LangChain itself is free; LangSmith (observability) from $39/month

tools.name: Portkey
tools.description: AI gateway and observability platform offering semantic caching, model routing with fallbacks, load balancing across multiple providers, and detailed cost analytics. Provides a unified API supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and 200+ models with automatic retry and failover logic.
tools.pricing_paid: Free tier available; Growth from $49/month; Enterprise custom

tools.name: Bifrost
tools.description: High-performance AI gateway designed for production LLM deployments, pairing semantic caching with provider-native prompt caching to achieve best-in-class combined savings. Handles routing, observability, and failover across major providers. Used in configurations where semantic caching and prompt caching complement each other.
tools.pricing_paid: Contact for pricing; designed for enterprise-scale deployments

tools.name: vLLM
tools.description: Open-source, high-throughput inference engine for self-hosted LLMs featuring PagedAttention for efficient KV cache management, continuous batching, and an OpenAI-compatible API server. The de facto standard for serving open-source models at production scale, enabling teams to avoid per-token API costs entirely.
tools.pricing_paid: Fully free and open-source; infrastructure costs are your own

tools.name: Cohere Rerank
tools.description: Cross-encoder reranking API that takes retrieved RAG chunks and re-scores them by true relevance to the query, allowing you to pass far fewer chunks to the LLM without losing answer quality. Reduces context tokens in RAG pipelines significantly. Also available as an open-source model for self-hosting.
tools.pricing_paid: Rerank API from $1 per 1,000 searches; free tier for development

tools.name: Maxim AI
tools.description: LLM evaluation and observability platform that also provides prompt optimization tooling and cost tracking per model, helping teams identify which prompts and models are underperforming on cost-efficiency. Supports production monitoring of cache hit rates and token usage across providers.
tools.pricing_paid: Free tier available; Pro and Enterprise tiers with custom pricing

quick_wins: Enable provider-native prompt caching immediately by moving your static system prompt and any shared context to the top of every request — this requires zero new infrastructure and can cut input costs by up to 90% on repeated prefixes with Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google.

Set explicit max_tokens limits on every API call and add 'be concise' or structured output instructions to your prompts — since output tokens cost 4–5x more than input tokens, a 30–50% reduction in output length has an outsized impact on your bill.

Submit all non-real-time workloads (document processing, batch evaluations, data enrichment) via the Anthropic or OpenAI Batch API to get an automatic 50% discount with no code changes beyond the API endpoint.

Audit and compress your system prompts to under 200 tokens by replacing verbose instructions with a single structured JSON schema and cutting redundant few-shot examples — a 30% prompt length reduction is a direct 30% input cost reduction.

Add a semantic caching layer (GPTCache, Redis Semantic Cache, or Helicone's built-in cache) in front of your highest-traffic LLM endpoint — even a 25–30% cache hit rate in a repetitive-query workload eliminates that fraction of API costs entirely while also reducing latency.
